news.title: South Korea's Lee to attend UN General Assembly, visit Mexico for Sheinbaum summit
news.text:
SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will visit the United States and ​Mexico on September 21 to 27 to attend the ‌UN General Assembly and hold a summit with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, the presidential Blue House said on Monday. Lee is also seeking meetings on ​the sidelines of the UN gathering with the leaders of ​the United States, Australia and other countries, the Blue ⁠House said.

A potential meeting with US President Donald Trump comes ​as Seoul and Washington negotiate details of South Korea’s $350 billion investment ​package in the United States under a trade deal struck by the allies last year.

South Korean officials told Reuters the talks were continuing, although Seoul ​postponed a parliamentary briefing on the plans scheduled for last ​week.

At the UN General Assembly, Lee is scheduled to deliver a keynote speech ‌on ⁠Tuesday on reforming the United Nations and outline his vision for peace and coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, according to the presidential office. He will also meet UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, his ​office said.

Lee will ​arrive in Mexico ⁠City on Wednesday and hold a summit with Sheinbaum the following day. After the summit, the ​leaders will have a joint press conference and ​oversee the ⁠signing of memorandums of understanding, Lee’s office said.

South Korea is seeking cooperation with Mexico in trade, energy, aerospace and culture, the Blue ⁠House ​said. Mexico is South Korea’s largest market ​for Kpop, while Seoul also sees opportunities to expand defence cooperation as Mexico modernises ​its military.

news.title: Xi rolls into Trump summit with China’s trade engine roaring
news.text:
BEIJING/WASHINGTON: In the four months since the leaders of the two global superpowers last met, Xi Jinping has overseen a surge in China’s trade with the world while Donald Trump has struggled with falling approval ​ratings at home.

That shift in fortunes has tempered expectations for their summit in Washington this week, analysts say, with Xi in no rush to make concessions and Trump constrained by a costly war with Iran that has hurt both his popularity and Americans’ wallets.

While thorny issues like Taiwan may surface, the main focus of the September 24 meeting is whether the leaders will signal an extension to a trade truce struck last year that averted a major shock to the global economy.

“Xi is not really looking for anything tangible. He wants to extend the gentleman’s agreement with Trump so that China has time to fortify itself,” said Jon Czin, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution who formerly served as China director at the US National Security Council.

’Living in Xi’s world’

White House officials have sought to downplay the potential for major breakthroughs. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng helmed preparatory talks in ‌New York on Sunday ‌aimed at teeing up some potential agreements on AI guardrails and trade in non-sensitive products.

That is a ​far ‌cry ⁠from Trump’s ​vow ⁠when he returned to office in 2025 to use tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China that was “killing” the United States.

But since agreeing the truce with Xi in October of that year, his attention has been divided among myriad other foreign policy battles, from the wars in Iran and Ukraine to disputes with Europe over free speech.

China has faced its own challenges, such as slowing domestic demand and a protracted property crisis, but the export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as China Shock 2.0.

China’s global trade surplus is on pace to top $1 trillion for a second straight year.

While US efforts to curb the cheap parcels that online retailers such as Shein and Temu rely on have worked, more than half of the roughly 6,500 product categories China ⁠sold to the US so far this year have grown compared to 2025.

A delegation of Chinese business leaders, ‌potentially including some firms facing US regulatory scrutiny as they seek greater market access, is set to ‌accompany Xi to Washington.

The Trump administration “thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to ​make concessions, and that did not occur,” said Scott Kennedy, an expert ‌on the US-China economic relationship at Washington-based think tank CSIS.

“Now this is Xi Jinping’s world, and we’re all living in it.”

Taiwan and trade wins

If Xi ‌is in the driver’s seat as analysts suggest, that will further unnerve US allies in Asia who expect the Chinese leader to push Trump to soften Washington’s support for Taiwan, the democratically governed island claimed by Beijing.

Xi repeatedly asked him about Taiwan when they met in Beijing in May, including about arms sales and Washington’s resolve to defend the island, Trump told reporters.

The US president described a pending $14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing.

Some officials in Taipei and Tokyo worry he may be ‌tempted to cash in that chip for political wins ahead of November’s midterm elections, which could prove challenging for his Republican Party.

That could include Chinese purchases of Boeing jets or farm goods, or commitments to curb the ⁠flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals that have ⁠fueled the US opioid crisis.

“China-US ties have become more transactional,” said Wu Xinbo, a professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University who advises China’s foreign ministry.

While Washington may want to prioritize trade talks, for Beijing, the US approach to Taiwan could be key, he said.

“If you accommodate our concern on the Taiwan issue, then we would be willing to accommodate your concerns on other issues, be it law enforcement or on purchases of US agricultural products,” Wu said.

Putting pressure on Iran

Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to bring an end to the war that has dragged Trump’s approval rating to the lowest of his political career.

However, Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Reuters earlier this month reported that Beijing is selling billions of dollars’ worth of goods to Iran through a sanctions-evasion scheme. China’s foreign ministry says it is not aware of such a scheme.

US threats last month of secondary sanctions on countries doing business with Iran — which Bessent called an “Economic D-Day” — appear not to have yet been wielded against Tehran’s largest trading partner.

That is more evidence, analysts say, that Trump is eager to keep relations with Xi steady as he focuses his energies elsewhere — an arrangement that also suits the Chinese leader.

“Both Xi ​and Trump feel it’s quite helpful to have stability in the relationship ​so that they can focus on more pressing things,” said Ruby Osman, senior geopolitical researcher at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

“For Trump, that is Iran. For Xi, that is building out China’s domestic resilience for whatever comes after Trump.”

news.title: Tech leads shares higher in Asia as oil slips
news.text:
SYDNEY: Share markets edged higher in Asia on Monday as AI’s insatiable demand for data buoyed chipmakers, and oil eased on reports more oil was finding its way ​out of the Middle East than previously thought despite the ongoing conflict in the Gulf.

Trade was thin with Japan on its Silver Week holiday ‌through to Wednesday, leaving the dollar easier at 156.67 yen with investors wary in case the Bank of Japan took advantage of the lack of liquidity to intervene in support of its currency.

The yen jumped on Friday after Japanese authorities conducted rate checks in the currency market, the Nikkei newspaper reported.

Japan’s Nikkei was shut but futures rose 0.5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy index gained 1.5%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares ​outside Japan rose 0.8%, and Chinese blue chips gained 0.6%.

S&P 500 futures firmed 0.4%, while Nasdaq futures added 0.6%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures and DAX ​futures both rose 0.4%, while FTSE futures firmed 0.2%.

Bond markets remained tense after a vicious selloff saw US 2-year yields jump 36 ⁠basis points in the past two weeks to heights not seen since mid-2024 at 4.7604%.

Hawkish guidance from the Federal Reserve last week has futures wagering on a 56% chance ​it will hike rates again in October, with a move by year-end considered a done deal.

“Tightening cycles are generally front-loaded, and the Fed almost never stops after one hike,” wrote ​analysts at BofA in a note. “With nominal consumer spending up 6.3% on the year, well above the 5% level historically associated with above-target core inflation, the Fed has little choice but to restrain demand.”

“Thus, we are retaining our call for just two more hikes, in October and December.”

Talk of increased supply hits oil

Central banks in the EU, UK, Japan, Australia and New Zealand are also expected to tighten ​again by year-end. The Swiss National Bank, Sweden’s Riksbank and Norges Bank hold policy meetings on Thursday, but all are seen holding steady for now.

Bonds have also been dogged ​by deficit worries with the risk premium on French debt spiking on Friday to its widest since the euro zone debt crisis.

German debt could come under pressure later on Monday after Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s mainstream ‌conservative party ⁠suffered its worst election results since 1949.

The news kept the euro flat at $1.1480 , having shed almost 1% last week as the dollar gained broadly.

Oil prices eased even as Iran and the United States exchanged new threats and after the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia’s capital. Brent fell 2.1% to $101.63 a barrel, while US crude dropped 2.1% to $98.15.

Data from analytics firm Kpler showed exports from the OPEC kingpin had recovered to just over 4 million barrels per day (bpd) so far in September after slumping to 2.4 million bpd in August, the lowest since at ​least 2013.

Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US ​Central Command, on the weekend said ⁠the volume of crude oil, cargo, and liquefied natural gas in the past two weeks was higher than at any point in the past six months.

There were also reports that Saudi Arabia was aiming to quickly restart some flows through its main east-to-west pipeline after it ​was damaged in attacks last week, though details were lacking.

“The closure of the East-West pipeline has materially altered the state of ​the oil market,” said ⁠Vivek Dhar, head of commodities at CBA.

“We now estimate that oil markets have 5 to 10 weeks before global oil and refined product inventories deplete, compared to estimates closer to 15 to 20 weeks just a fortnight ago.”

This would increase pressure on Washington to make a deal with Iran, at least to boost flows through the Strait of Hormuz and keep the Bab ⁠el-Mandeb passage open, ​he added.

US President Donald Trump will be attending the United Nations General Assembly this week, ahead of ​a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng concluded talks in New York on Sunday, with the US side proposing a new AI safety notification mechanism for ​the leaders to consider at their summit.

In other commodity markets, the rise in yields hampered non-interest-paying gold, which was flat at $4,380 an ounce .

news.title: EAM Jaishankar arrives in Zurich, briefed on India-Switzerland-Liechtenstein ties ahead of UNGA visit
news.text:
Zurich, Sep 21 (IANS) External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar arrived at Zurich airport on Monday en route to New York, where he will lead the Indian delegation to the high-level week of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

The Embassy of India in Switzerland and the Principality of Liechtenstein shared an update on X, saying Ambassador Kumar warmly welcomed Jaishankar at the airport. The ambassador also briefed the External Affairs Minister on the latest developments in relations involving India, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, including recent high-level visits.

“Amb Kumar warmly welcomed Hon’ble EAM @DrSJaishankar at Zurich airport en route to his official visit to New York to participate in UN General Assembly-2026. Amb Kumar also briefed Hon’ble EAM on the latest developments including high-level visits between India, Switzerland and Liechtenstein,” the embassy said in its post.

EAM Jaishankar is travelling to New York for the annual UNGA high-level session, with his address to the General Assembly scheduled for September 26. 

The Ministry of External Affairs, announcing his visit, said: “EAM, S. Jaishankar will be leading the Indian delegation for the high-level week at the 81st session of the UNGA, New York, USA. The EAM’s address at the high-level session of the 81st United Nations General Assembly is scheduled for September 26.”

His visit comes amid heightened diplomatic attention on India-US relations following the passage of US legislation granting President Donald Trump expanded powers to impose tariffs on countries purchasing Russian energy.

The US House of Representatives recently passed the legislation, which allows for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. President Trump subsequently signed the Russia sanctions bill into law. 

New Delhi has said it remains committed to safeguarding its energy requirements while maintaining diversified sources of supply. Following the passage of the legislation, the Ministry of External Affairs said India “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” and would continue diversified sourcing based on evolving market dynamics. 

Against this backdrop, EAM Jaishankar’s presence in New York for UNGA is expected to provide an opportunity for India to engage with a range of international counterparts.

His visit follows the Zurich stop, where discussions also covered developments in India’s ties with Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

news.title: ‘Peace track our number one priority’: Zelensky says Trump meeting could change a lot
news.text:
Washington, Sep 21 (IANS) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that he and US President Donald Trump had agreed to meet in New York, and said Ukraine was ready to take serious steps towards peace in coordination with the American team.

“We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelensky said in a post on X after speaking with Trump.

He did not announce a date for the meeting or specify what the two leaders hoped to agree. His account outlined areas under discussion but did not announce a peace agreement or a timetable for implementing any measures.

Zelensky described the conversation as important and said it had covered substantial ground. He placed the pursuit of peace at the centre of Ukraine’s engagement with the American team.

“The peace track is our number one priority,” he said.

The Ukrainian president identified energy security, food security and the protection of human life as issues being considered alongside possible steps to reduce tensions. He did not set out the individual proposals or explain how they would be put into practice.

“There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life,” he said.

Zelensky also signalled Ukraine’s willingness to act, saying work with US officials was continuing.

“We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps,” he said.

He did not identify those steps or say whether they would require reciprocal action. The post did not set out any commitments by Russia.

Zelensky thanked Trump for a visit to Kyiv by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said the visit had allowed detailed discussions and given the two Americans a direct view of conditions in Ukraine.

“We went through the key details thoroughly, and they saw the situation in Ukraine firsthand,” he said.

Separately, Zelensky thanked the US president for signing legislation he referred to as the Lindsey Graham bill into law.

“I thanked the American President for signing the Lindsey Graham bill into law,” he said.

The post did not give the legislation’s formal title, describe its provisions or explain how it related to the diplomatic steps under discussion.

“We all concur – there must be peace. Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine! Thank you to everyone who’s helping!” he said.

news.title: Oil hits over 1-week low on hopes of boost to diplomacy in Iran war
news.text:
SINGAPORE: Oil prices slid to their ​lowest in more than a week on Monday on hopes diplomacy in the Iran war will get a chance ‌this week amid a UN meet and as investors eyed a partial recovery in shipments from Saudi Arabia despite ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

Brent crude futures and US West Texas Intermediate crude touched their lowest since September 10 earlier on Monday, with Brent at $101.71 a barrel by 0213 GMT, down $2.16, or ​2.08%, after settling 0.91% lower on Friday.

US West Texas Intermediate crude lost $2.15, or 2.14%, to $98.15 a barrel following a 1.58% ​drop in the previous session.

“It seems that a degree of risk premium is being removed from ⁠oil prices on hopes that a diplomatic path to de-escalate the US-Iran war may arrive this week,” Tim Waterer, chief market analyst ​at KCM Trade, said.

“Whether that hope proves to be warranted or not is another question. Time will tell.”

The WTI broke a key ​psychological support at $100 a barrel while some investors may have rolled over their positions in the October contract a day ahead of expiry to November, a Singapore-based broker said.

Iran and the US exchanged new threats on Sunday amid the stalemate, although President Donald Trump said he would be open to meeting Iranian ​President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly.

Iran has conveyed its conditions ​to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations aimed at ending the war with the US, Al Jazeera cited Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, as saying in ‌an interview ⁠on Saturday.

However, tensions in the Middle East remained elevated as Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital of Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

China has asked Iran to help rein in the Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the attacks, according ​to three Iranian sources familiar ​with the matter.

The attacks by ⁠the Houthis on Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline have prompted the state energy firm to increase exports through the Strait of Hormuz this month and next after halting some shipments via Yanbu.

That enabled exports from the OPEC kingpin ​to recover to over 4 million barrels per day (bpd) so far in September after slumping to ​2.4 million bpd ⁠in August, the lowest since at least 2013, according to provisional data from analytics firm Kpler.

“Middle East oil flows remain surprisingly strong despite the disruption to Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline,” JPMorgan analysts said in a September 18 note, adding that the total oil flows averaged 17.1 million ⁠bpd in ​the past 10 days, just 6.1 million bpd below the 2025 average.

“The most ​notable pivot has come from Saudi Arabia,” the analysts said, as satellite data indicated Saudi oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 2.9 million bpd over ​the past six days, up from just 700,000 bpd in August.

news.title: Iran-US Tensions Escalate as Tehran Refuses Strait of Hormuz Reopening Without Conditions
news.text:
Iran has ruled out reopening the Strait of Hormuz or returning to the previous framework of negotiations with the United States until Washington meets conditions set by Tehran, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday. Ghalibaf said Iran had communicated its demands to the US through intermediaries and would not change its position until Tehran's conditions were fulfilled and what it described as the country's rights were recognised.

“Until these conditions are met, the legitimate rights of the Iranian nation are recognised, and the Americans’ commitments are implemented,” there would be no return to the previous negotiation framework or reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, Ghalibaf said, according to Iranian media. US-Iran Talks: Qatar Says Washington Wants Agreement With Tehran.

Iran Links Hormuz Reopening to US Commitments

The Strait of Hormuz has become a central point of contention in the escalating confrontation between Tehran and Washington. The strategic waterway is a major route for global energy shipments, making restrictions on maritime traffic a concern for oil supplies and international trade.

Iran has maintained that the waterway will remain closed until its demands are addressed. Tehran and Washington had reached an agreement in June that included provisions linked to ending military operations and reopening the strait, but the arrangement later broke down amid disagreements over navigation and security arrangements.

Iranian officials have also said that Tehran's conditions for ending the conflict were conveyed to Washington through Qatar. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei previously said the demands included an end to the war on all fronts, the release of Iran's frozen funds and an end to the US naval blockade. US Issues 'Do Not Travel' Advisory for Iran Amid Escalating West Asian Tensions.

Tehran Rules Out Immediate Return to Negotiations

Ghalibaf's latest comments indicate that Iran is not prepared to resume the earlier negotiation framework without action from Washington. The remarks came amid continuing diplomatic activity around the conflict. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is expected to stop in Doha for consultations before travelling to New York for the UN General Assembly, with regional developments and the Strait of Hormuz among the issues under discussion.

US President Donald Trump has also indicated that he could be open to discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the UN General Assembly, although the two sides remain far apart on the terms for negotiations.

US Moves to Enforce Maritime Blockade

The standoff has also affected commercial shipping in and around the region. The US Central Command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels as of September 20 as part of efforts to enforce its maritime restrictions involving Iran. The move comes as Washington continues to maintain pressure on Iranian maritime traffic.

Iranian officials have meanwhile warned against any renewed US military action. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters said that any new US attack would trigger strikes against American bases and interests across the region. Tehran also warned regional countries against supporting any US military operation against Iran. The latest developments leave the Strait of Hormuz at the centre of the broader US-Iran confrontation, with Tehran tying any reopening of the strategic waterway and return to negotiations to the fulfilment of its stated conditions.

news.title: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles into East Sea
news.text:
SEOUL: North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles into the sea off its eastern coast on Sunday, South Korea’s military said, with the second flying more than 600 kilometres.

The launches came days after Pyongyang reasserted its status as a nuclear-armed state and rejected a United Nations resolution demanding it halt its nuclear activities.

South Korea’s military said the first missile was launched at around 3pm from the Wonsan area and flew around 450 kilometres into the East Sea, a body of water also called the Sea of Japan.

“Our military detected an additional short-range ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea at around 5:50pm,” South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said.

The second missile “flew more than 600 kilometres, and South Korean and US authorities are conducting a detailed analysis to determine its exact specifications,” it said.

The JCS said South Korea, the United States and Japan had been “tracking and sharing relevant developments from the initial stage of the launch”. Japan lodged a “stern protest” with North Korea over the launches, condemning them as a threat to regional peace and security, the Kyodo news agency cited the government as saying.

South Korea’s presidential National Security Office convened an emergency security meeting following the first launch and assessed its impact on national security, the presidential office said.

The government called on Pyongyang to “immediately cease” its ballistic missile launches, describing Sunday’s firings as a “grave act” that violated UN Security Council resolutions.

‘Absolute’ status

The launches came eight days after North Korea fired multiple short-range ballistic missiles towards the East Sea as part of what it later described as a joint firepower drill.

That exercise involved long-range artillery and missiles, with the weapons “hitting the targets with 100 percent accuracy”, state media reported.

North Korea accused “hostile forces” of seeking to end the country’s nuclear programme during this week’s General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

A foreign ministry spokesperson said the IAEA resolution “has no effect on the DPRK’s position as a nuclear weapons state”, using the acronym for North Korea’s official name.

The North’s status as a nuclear power is “guaranteed by the actual nuclear deterrent and irreversibly and permanently fixed by the supreme law of the state”, the spokesperson said. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, recently said the country’s nuclear-armed status was “absolute” and called those hoping for its denuclearisation “idiots”.

US President Donald Trump said in August that North Korea possessed 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons, while South Korea has put the figure at between 80 and 120.

news.title: US, China discuss AI safety ahead of Trump-Xi summit
news.text:
US and Chinese economic officials discussed creating a communication channel for AI concerns at meetings Sunday as they set the stage for a summit of the countries' top leaders this week.

"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters after long talks with a team led by Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.

The talks are a prelude to a planned White House meeting on Thursday of the leaders of the world's two biggest economies: US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The discussions, which also included the top US trade official Jamieson Greer, lasted around eight hours at JPMorgan Chase's headquarters in New York.

Bessant said the two sides discussed setting up a way to communicate about AI issues called the "US-China AI dialogue."

"The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries," Bessent said.

Such notifications are for potential "incidents," or a situation "that rises up to a national security level from AI," he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.

Bessent and He also spoke one-on-one during the day, a source familiar with the matter said.

Chinese official Li Chenggang, who was elevated to a top-level international trade representative post shortly before the meetings, was present in the New York talks too. But the Chinese delegation did not address reporters.

Greer stressed Sunday it is "imperative that we are able to work together."

Both sides are looking to ease tensions on trade, technology and other strategic concerns. These include the possible extension of a trade truce and guardrails for AI development.

Non-sensitive trade

Asked about the possibility of mutual tariff reduction on certain goods, Greer said teams "are continuing to work through this."

The aim is to identify "non-sensitive" goods that can be considered separately from trade measures in the future, he added.

Such products could cover consumer goods from the Chinese side and energy, agriculture and other products like medical devices on the US side.

Beyond less sensitive items, US officials are also seeking to ensure the continued flow of rare earth magnets and critical minerals that are vital for US manufacturers.

Working level meetings could continue into Monday, a source familiar with discussions earlier told AFP.

Previous negotiations saw China pledge purchases of US agriculture goods too, and their fulfilment of the terms could also be an issue under scrutiny.

Another issue is US economic pressure on Iran, as Washington's war with Tehran has entered its seventh month.

China is a top economic partner of Iran that buys much of its oil output and a key diplomatic backer.

Analysts caution that expectations for the Trump-Xi summit are low.

"One of the only things we can hope for in the short term is a truce, and that this will likely continue through the remainder of this year," said former US deputy secretary of state Kurt Campbell.

"I think you will hear the president announce the intention to meet with Xi Jinping two more times," added Campbell, who is now chairman of The Asia Group consultancy.

Trump and Xi are expected to meet in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, China. Trump is also anticipated to invite Xi to the G20 summit in December at his Doral resort in Miami.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
news.summary: US and Chinese officials discussed creating a mechanism to communicate over potentially serious AI incidents during talks in New York on Sunday, as the two sides sought progress on technology and trade ahead of this week’s Trump-Xi summit.

news.title: Forensic psychiatrist flags 'dangerous' signs of Trump's mental decline: 'Alarming'
news.text:
A prominent forensic psychiatrist flagged disturbing new signs that President Donald Trump's mental state continues to decline. 

Dr. Bandy Lee, president of the World Mental Health Coalition, argued during a new episode of MeidasTouch's "The Weekend Show" that Trump's recent attempt to wrap himself up in the tragedy of 9/11 shows how "fragile he is in his sense of self." 

During the recent 9/11 commemoration ceremony, Trump claimed that first responders pulled him from the rubble of one of the World Trade Center buildings. He also claimed he sent teams to help respond to the tragedy. Fact-checkers have declared both claims to be untrue. 

Lee argued that Trump's claims are similar to what a toddler would do when trying to be "king or queen of the universe."

"It is abnormal and pathological when it involves a fully-grown adult, whether it is because of arrested development or because one has regressed to that state," Lee said. 

Questions about Trump's mental fitness have swirled throughout his second administration. Trump has been photographed sleeping in the Oval Office during press events, and his right side has drooped in recent public appearances. 

Lee noted that Trump's decision to continue lying about the events of 9/11 shows the amount of cognitive stress he's under. Polling has shown Democrats have a momentum advantage heading into the midterms, and the war in Iran continues to hurt the American economy, she noted. 

Lee also pointed to the memes that Trump has posted online, especially the one of him driving a spaceship and blowing up the entire world, as "alarming indications of how endangered he feels psychologically and how he needs to fight back, and become the most powerful and dangerous person on the planet."

"That is where his mind is going," Lee said. 

Lee added that Trump's mental state has put the world in an "extremely dangerous" situation because Trump may be willing to use devastating force in order to save his self-image. 

"The setup that we have is that we have no way of countermanding a, fit or not ... there's no way to countermand a nuclear weapon," Lee said.

news.title: Trump mulls next moves on Iran amid ominous warnings
news.text:
State Dept warns Americans to brace for ‘unforeseen escalation’ across the Middle East• Trump abruptly leaves Camp David; tells Fox News ‘if and when I blow entire nation up is my question’; claims Houthis agreed not to fight US• Iran threatens ‘sustained retaliation’; says Washington allies will be considered party to conflict• PM Shehbaz to highlight mediatory role at UNGA, says envoy

WASHINGTON: The United States issued fresh security warnings for Americans in the Middle East on Sunday, cautioning that the security environment remained volatile and could face an “unforeseen escalation” as President Donald Trump considers his next steps in the war with Iran.

Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, returning unannounced to the White House on Saturday evening as the White House offered no explanation for the abrupt change of plan, which comes just days before he is due in New York for the UN General Assembly.

The warnings, circulated through US diplomatic missions in the region, urged Americans currently in the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

Americans outside the region were advised to “seriously reconsider travel to and through the region”.

“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation,” the State Department said in its alerts.

“Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly.”

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also cut short his US visit and returned to Israel, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the region.

Trump’s next move

Trump has indicated that he faces a major decision over whether to intensify the conflict. The US president told Fox News that he is in “deciding mode” on Iran and “big things will be happening in the not-so-distant future”.

According to network’s Trey Yingst, the president outlined the options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal”. Trump reportedly added, “My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They [Iranians] better behave.”

When asked about meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who will be attending the UN General Assembly in New York this week, Trump said he would ‘probably be open’ to it.

In an interview with Axios earlier this week, Trump said: “I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them, or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me.”

On the other hand, Trump reiterated that Houthis agreed not to attack the United States, Fox News reported.

He also claimed a week ago the Houthis were holding back from attacking US forces in the region. “The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland on Sept 12. “They don’t want us to go after them.”

Sustained retaliation

Meanwhile, Iran warned on Sunday against any big new attack by the US and its allies, saying it had information such a move was being prepared, adding to the anxiety in a region already on edge.

Iran’s military central command said on state media that any new attack would trigger sustained retaliation against US bases and interests and that Washington’s regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict. It did not elaborate on the information it said it had about a coming US attack.

Mediatory role

Meanwhile, briefing journalists ahead of the 81st UN General Assembly session, Pakistan’s Ambassador to the UN Asim Iftikhar Ahmad said that Islamabad will stress its mediatory role amid the widening Middle East crisis during the high-level week of the UN General Assembly.

He said that PM Shehbaz Sharif’s address on the 25th would present Pakistan’s perspective on the evolving regional and international security environment and emphasising dialogue, diplomacy, restraint and the peaceful resolution of disputes.

Pakistan, the ambassador said, would also use the high-level week to underline its constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability and its resolve to work with UN member states to uphold the UN Charter, strengthen multilateralism, prevent conflict and advance international cooperation.

news.title: Iran rules out Hormuz reopening until US meets conditions; US redirects 109 vessels near Strait to enforce blockade
news.text: Iran has ruled out reopening the Strait of Hormuz or returning to the previous framework of negotiations with the United States until Washington meets Tehran’s conditions, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said, amid heightened tensions between the two countries.Iran has conveyed its demands to the US through intermediaries and would not reconsider its position until those conditions were met, Ghalibaf said.“Our messages and conditions have been conveyed explicitly to the other side through intermediaries. And until these conditions are met, the inalienable rights of the Iranian nation are recognised, and the Americans fulfil their commitments, there will be no possibility of a return to the previous negotiation framework or to reopen the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.The Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy shipments, has become a major flashpoint in the confrontation, with restrictions on maritime traffic raising concerns over disruptions to oil supplies and international trade.The remarks came after Iran's central military command warned that any renewed US military action would trigger attacks on American bases and interests across the region.The Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters said in a statement carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA that any US military action would be met with “continuous, effective and painful” attacks.“Should the United States make any mistake against the Islamic Republic of Iran, all its bases and interests in the region will be targeted in continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitation or consideration,” the statement said.The Iranian military command also warned countries in the region against supporting any US military operation, saying those that assist Washington would be treated as participants in the action.. Meanwhile, the US Central Command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels as part of efforts to enforce Washington’s naval blockade on Iran.“A U.S. Sailor stands watch aboard USS John Paul Jones (DDG 53). As of Sept. 20, CENTCOM forces have redirected 109 commercial vessels to ensure total compliance,” CENTCOM said in a post on X.. The U.S. military resumed enforcement of the blockade on maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports on July 14.U.S. President Donald Trump has warned Tehran of significant consequences if it refuses to alter its behaviour, while indicating that he could be open to talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the UN General Assembly in New York.Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei had earlier said Tehran had conveyed, through Qatari mediation, conditions for ending the conflict, including an end to hostilities on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the naval blockade.The developments come as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly, with the U.S.-Iran confrontation and the wider tensions in West Asia expected to figure prominently in discussions.(With inputs from ANI) .Iran says new 'prohibited zone' extends beyond Hormuz into parts of Arabian Sea.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Houthis vow to spare foreign ships after seizing key Red Sea chokepoint
news.text:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have vowed not to target countries other than Saudi Arabia after their forces captured strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, an important shipping chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.

The Houthis, an Iran-backed Shiite group, declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia earlier this year, accusing the kingdom of imposing an illegal “siege” on the territories under their control.

“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” Houthi political spokesman Mohamed al-Bukhaiti told AP in an interview published on Sunday.

“The goal of our military operations is not to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but rather to ensure freedom of navigation through it for everyone, including Yemen,” he added.

Al-Bukhaiti confirmed indirect contacts with the US through Oman. According to earlier media reports, Saudi Arabia had asked President Donald Trump to intervene militarily, but the US has so far limited its cooperation to intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.

The Houthis seized the port of Mokha and strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, earlier this month, inflicting heavy casualties on Saudi-backed government forces. The rebels have also fired drones and missiles at Saudi cities, including the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh.

The escalation comes as the Strait of Hormuz, the other major maritime chokepoint linking the Middle East with global markets, remains effectively closed to most commercial shipping amid the US-Iran conflict.

Saudi Arabia first launched a military intervention on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in 2015, following the fall of the capital, Sanaa, to the Houthis the previous year.

Large-scale fighting in Yemen largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but erupted again after September 8 strikes on Sanaa airport aimed at preventing an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the attacks, which the kingdom attributed to Yemeni government forces.

The US State Department issued security alerts across the Middle East on Saturday night, warning of a potential escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, as well as possible attacks on American diplomatic facilities. According to CNN, Trump was briefed on potential strike options in Yemen but has not authorized military action.

The Houthis reached a separate ceasefire with the US in May 2025, under which Washington halted its air campaign in Yemen and the group agreed to stop targeting US vessels in the Red Sea.

Yemen’s Houthis have vowed to target only Saudi-linked vessels after seizing strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait

news.title: Trump administration readies sweeping sanctions against ICC, reports say  - Bahamas Spectator – Bahamas
news.text:
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) that could disrupt the tribunal’s finances and day-to-day operations.

The US sanctions would prohibit most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

The move would mark a sharp escalation in Washington’s campaign against the Hague-based court by targeting the institution itself rather than individual judges and prosecutors.

The Trump administration plans to announce the sanctions soon, according to the Reuters news agency, quoting two sources familiar with the matter.

The Journal, citing anonymous officials, said a decision could be finalised during this week’s United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York or soon afterwards.

If imposed, the measures would generally bar US citizens and companies from providing the ICC with money, goods or services without a licence from the US Treasury.

Banks and other companies often take an especially cautious approach to US sanctions because they rely on access to the American financial system.

The ICC president and registrar have previously warned that sanctions on the organisation as a whole could interfere with its ability to buy information technology and insurance services, hire investigators and make routine payments, including salaries for American employees.

The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.

Washington has already sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025.

In August, it added the court’s President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye to the list, with restrictions on them taking effect on September 17.

The United States has never joined the court.

The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members.

Relations deteriorated sharply after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Israel, like the US, is not an ICC member and rejects the court’s jurisdiction.

Washington has also objected to an earlier ICC investigation into alleged abuses in Afghanistan involving US personnel.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a campaign in July to further isolate the court and urged other countries to withdraw from it.

Trump’s move adds to growing opposition to the ICC in recent months.

Chad and Venezuela moved in July to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.

Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration in August, arguing that existing sanctions obstruct their legal and human rights work.

news.title: US-Iran Talks: Qatar Says Washington Wants Agreement With Tehran
news.text:
Qatar says it has been working with the United States and Iran to revive negotiations, with mediators exchanging proposals for nearly two weeks and shuttling between regional capitals. Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said Doha has received assurances from US officials that Washington wants to reach an agreement with Tehran.

The latest diplomatic effort comes amid continued tensions between Washington and Tehran, particularly over the Strait of Hormuz and the broader regional conflict. Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in mediation efforts aimed at bringing the two sides back to negotiations.

Qatar Pushes to Resume US-Iran Talks

Al-Ansari said Qatar has been exchanging ideas with both Washington and Tehran for almost two weeks in an attempt to determine whether formal talks can resume. “Our mediators are currently moving between different capitals in the hope of making progress,” he said, according to Qatari media. Qatar's mediation comes as diplomatic channels remain open despite significant differences between the two sides. Doha has previously played a role in facilitating communication between Washington and Tehran. Donald Trump Says He’s in ‘Deciding Mode’ on Iran, Warns of ‘Very Big Things’ As Tehran Sends 7 Conditions.

US Has Signalled Interest in Agreement

According to al-Ansari, Qatari officials have received assurances from members of the US administration that Washington wants to reach an agreement with Iran. The statement indicates that the US remains open to a negotiated outcome, although no new agreement has been announced and major issues between the two countries remain unresolved. US President Donald Trump has also indicated that he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New York during the United Nations General Assembly this week.

Iran Sends Conditions Through Qatar

The latest mediation effort follows Iran's communication of conditions for returning to negotiations through Qatari intermediaries. Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran wants an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the US naval blockade. He also said Tehran was awaiting Trump's response.

Iranian officials have continued to link the future of negotiations to the situation around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy shipments. Iran has maintained that the waterway will not return to normal operations until its stated conditions and what it describes as US commitments are addressed. US Issues 'Do Not Travel' Advisory for Iran Amid Escalating West Asian Tensions.

Strait of Hormuz Remains Key Issue

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the central issues in the standoff between Iran and the US. Qatar has called for an international understanding to protect waterways and has warned against using strategic shipping routes as a political or military tool. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was also due to stop in Doha for consultations before travelling to New York for the UN General Assembly, highlighting Qatar's continuing role in the diplomatic efforts.

What Happens Next

For now, Qatar's efforts appear focused on creating conditions for Washington and Tehran to return to direct negotiations. The exchange of proposals does not amount to a new agreement, and differences over the war, sanctions, frozen Iranian assets, the naval blockade and the Strait of Hormuz remain significant. The coming diplomatic contacts in New York, alongside Qatar and Pakistan's mediation, could provide another channel for discussions as both sides consider their next steps.

news.title: EAM Jaishankar arrives in Zurich, briefed on India-Switzerland-Liechtenstein ties ahead of UNGA visit
news.text: Digital Desk | Zurich, Sep 21 (IANS) External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar arrived at Zurich airport on Monday en route to New York, where he will lead the Indian delegation to the high-level week of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). The Embassy of India in Switzerland and the Principality of Liechtenstein shared an update on X, saying Ambassador Kumar warmly welcomed Jaishankar at the airport. The ambassador also briefed the External Affairs Minister on the latest developments in relations involving India, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, including recent high-level visits. “Amb Kumar warmly welcomed Hon’ble EAM @DrSJaishankar at Zurich airport en route to his official visit to New York to participate in UN General Assembly-2026. Amb Kumar also briefed Hon’ble EAM on the latest developments including high-level visits between India, Switzerland and Liechtenstein,” the embassy said in its post. EAM Jaishankar is travelling to New York for the annual UNGA high-level session, with his address to the General Assembly scheduled for September 26. The Ministry of External Affairs, announcing his visit, said: “EAM, S. Jaishankar will be leading the Indian delegation for the high-level week at the 81st session of the UNGA, New York, USA. The EAM’s address at the high-level session of the 81st United Nations General Assembly is scheduled for September 26.” His visit comes amid heightened diplomatic attention on India-US relations following the passage of US legislation granting President Donald Trump expanded powers to impose tariffs on countries purchasing Russian energy. The US House of Representatives recently passed the legislation, which allows for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. President Trump subsequently signed the Russia sanctions bill into law. New Delhi has said it remains committed to safeguarding its energy requirements while maintaining diversified sources of supply. Following the passage of the legislation, the Ministry of External Affairs said India “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” and would continue diversified sourcing based on evolving market dynamics. Against this backdrop, EAM Jaishankar’s presence in New York for UNGA is expected to provide an opportunity for India to engage with a range of international counterparts. His visit follows the Zurich stop, where discussions also covered developments in India’s ties with Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

news.title: As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
news.text:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.
However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.
By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.
That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing.
Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began.
The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push.

The cloud escape hatch
Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers.
“For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.”
To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year.
Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring.
Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data.

To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024.
However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing.
The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access.
“If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said.
Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners.
The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power.
The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”.
Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained.
“Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added.
Southeast Asia’s data centre boom
If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs.
Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda.

Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market.
Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry.
If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market
Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group
“If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries.
Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.”
The region also offers competitive energy economics.
In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining.
While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News.
Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep.
Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”.

The domestic bottleneck
For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale.
Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported.
The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only.
For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing.
The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities.
ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August.
“There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution.
Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter.
Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally.
Accelerating self-reliance
If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs.
Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity.
“Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products.
Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier.
Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year.
The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.

However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August.
Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang.
Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report.
That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank.
As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.
However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

news.title: In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way
news.text:
It’s not just his name; court documents show Trump is insisting on three things. One is changing the plaque on the front of the building to read: “The John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts, renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump.”

Second, when his Trump Kennedy Centre Fund reaches an endowment of $US100 million, he proposes to add: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Centre Fund” to the plaque. Finally, he wants to name the surrounding area “President Donald J. Trump Plaza”. The board approved these proposals last month.

Last week, a federal judge appointed by Barack Obama, Christopher Cooper, put a stop to this. He is the same judge who last year ordered Trump’s name be taken off the building, as Congress had named it in honour of President Kennedy alone. Now, he said, the administration “plays word games” to try to skirt the ruling.

“Alone means alone,” Cooper ruled. “The board cannot honour both President Kennedy and President Trump without running afoul of the terms of the injunction and the board’s own governing statute.”
news.summary: The Kennedy Centre was once America’s cultural heart. Now it is barricaded, empty and being held hostage as the US president insists his name be added to its facade.

news.title: China Rare-Earth Magnet Exports To US Drop Before Xi-Trump Meet
news.text: China's exports of rare-earth magnets to the US fell last month, ahead of a meeting between the leaders of the countries that will probably involve discussions on flows of critical minerals.Shipments of magnets to the US dropped 21% in August to 512 tons from the month before, according to Chinese customs data released on Sunday. The industrial components - along with other types of rare-earth products - became Beijing's greatest point of leverage over Washington in trade negotiations last year.President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are due to meet in the US capital on Thursday to flesh out how the world's two biggest economies will manage everything from trade to artificial intelligence. China hopes to offer more licenses for rare earth exports as a bargaining chip in talks, people with familiar with the matter said, without disclosing what Beijing would demand in return."Washington needs stability with Beijing to keep these critical inputs moving," Chris Kennedy, lead for economic statecraft at Bloomberg Economics, said in a note. "Yet periods of calm that restore access to lower-cost Chinese material weaken the urgency for the US to break its dependence on China."ALSO READ: ACFI Seeks Rs 5,000-7,500 Crore Scheme To Reduce China Dependence In Crop ProtectionChina imposed controls on exports of rare-earth magnets - used in everything from cars to consumer goods and weaponry - in April 2025, although they were subsequently eased. The industry is keenly waiting for the outcome of the Xi-Trump talks as they come before the expiration of a US-China trade truce, which includes commitments by Beijing to maintain flows of critical minerals by issuing more generous export licenses, in November.Shipments slumped in May last year, but quickly recovered. They're running at an average of about 504 tons a month this year, although that's still below 621 tons in 2024 before the curbs. Chinese customs data shows that direct exports of rare earths including yttrium, dysprosium and terbium - subject to export controls - have also dropped compared with previous years.ALSO READ: Inside Trump's AI Vision: Data Centre Push, White House AI 'Czar,' And Keeping China At BayIn May, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer gave Beijing a "passing grade" for its performance in keeping flows of critical minerals going. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that China should "fully meet its commitments." Bessent and China's Vice Premier He Lifeng held talks in New York over the weekend ahead of the leaders' meeting.(This story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: US issues travel alert,  Iran warns of renewed strikes as fears of wider conflict loom over West Asia
news.text:
Fears of wider escalation and a surge in violence loom across West Asia after the US issued travel advisory warning Americans in the region of a possible rapid deterioration in the security situation amid Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia. The alert comes as Iran claims Washington is preparing to renew its bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic, fuelling uncertainty over the US administration’s next move. The warning comes ahead of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York, amid growing uncertainty over Washington’s next move.
Amid heightened tensions in West Asia , the US Virtual Embassy in Iran, on Monday, has issued a security alert urging American citizens not to travel to Iran “for any reason” and advising those already in the country to leave.
In another alert, issued a day earlier, US said, "Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation. Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
Adding to the uncertainty, President Donald Trump abruptly ended a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday without an official explanation. Around the same time, the US State Department issued a new security alert for American citizens across West Asia.
Trump has reportedly kept several options on the table. Speaking to a Fox News reporter, he said “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and listed the choices as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that any US attack would trigger sustained retaliation against American interests in the region.
“All US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations,” the IRGC said.
Iranian leaders also warned that any response could reach US naval forces in the Indian Ocean. They accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing”, alleging that they had approved US attacks.
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Tehran would pursue both military action and diplomacy, arguing that Iran must fight its adversaries while also negotiating when the timing is appropriate.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia raise regional tensions
Fears of a wider escalation in West Asia are growing after Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, on Saturday. The strikes marked the first sustained assault on Aramco oil facilities in the capital since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire collapsed in June.
Saudi authorities said they had intercepted the missiles. However, photographs from the area showed smoke rising from an Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, a key route for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.
The US largely considers the Houthis an Iranian proxy force and maintains that attacks on Riyadh could not take place without approval from Tehran. Iran has rejected that claim.
The developments have also raised questions over Washington’s willingness to provide direct military support to its regional allies. Last week, Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US military assistance.
Saudi Arabia had sought support after the Houthis made a sudden advance and seized strategic ports along Yemen’s western coastline. The move gave the group control over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a narrow maritime passage used by commercial vessels travelling through the Red Sea towards Asia.
Hormuz disruption adds to pressure on energy supplies
Further east, the Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, is already effectively closed to western shipping. The disruption has increased pressure on European energy supplies, prompting countries such as France to introduce emergency measures aimed at preventing fuel shortages.
The Houthis had previously assured US officials that they would restrict their attacks to Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea, in an effort to keep Washington from becoming directly involved in the conflict with Saudi Arabia. Trump appeared to consider those assurances sufficient to protect essential US interests and avoid military intervention.
The Pentagon’s budget pressures and declining munitions stocks, following the conflict with Iran, have also contributed to US reluctance to expand the war, according to a report. Repeated bombing campaigns have failed to dislodge the Houthis, whose rapid advance towards the Red Sea coast caught Saudi-backed Yemeni forces off guard.
Trump played down the possibility of a wider confrontation with the group in an interview with Fox News.
“The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US,” he said.
The Houthi government said 318 ships had travelled through the strait between September 10 and 18.

news.title: Iran rules out reopening Strait of Hormuz, returning to US talks until conditions met

Iran’s Armed Forces spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi said the initiative in the strategic waterway remained with Iran’s armed forces, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency. He also rejected US statements on maritime traffic through the strait as a psychological operation.Iran has also issued fresh warnings over possible US military action. The Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters said any renewed US attack would trigger attacks against American bases and interests across the region, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.“Should the United States make any mistake against the Islamic Republic of Iran, all its bases and interests in the region will be targeted in continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitation or consideration,” the military command said.The Iranian command also warned regional countries against supporting any US military operation against Tehran, saying countries that assist Washington would be considered participants in the action, according to IRNA.Meanwhile, US central command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels as part of efforts to enforce Washington’s naval blockade against Iran. CENTCOM said the vessels were redirected as of September 20 to ensure compliance with the blockade.The US military resumed enforcement of the naval blockade against maritime traffic entering and leaving Iranian ports on July 14, according to CENTCOM.US President Donald Trump has meanwhile warned Iran of consequences if Tehran refuses to change its position, while also indicating that he could be open to talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the UN General Assembly in New York.The latest developments come as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly, with the US-Iran confrontation and wider West Asia tensions expected to remain major issues during the diplomatic gathering.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
