news.title: Carney touts Arctic alliance with Norway during PM's visit to Ottawa, amid Russia threat
news.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his focus on building international relationships, including with Norway, is part of the answer to renewed threats from Russia.

During a news conference with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Ottawa on Sunday, both leaders were asked about warnings from the Polish prime minister that Russia may be planning attacks on European countries that support Ukraine.

Støre said those warnings should be taken seriously and that Norway's intelligence has concluded there are "real threats coming from hybrid activity, ranging all the way to potential sabotage."

Carney didn't comment on the credibility of the threats but said he agreed with Støre's statements.

"One of the advantages of this relationship and deepening across a broad range of relationships is, yes, greater intelligence sharing, greater perspective, greater capacities that are built together," he said.

Carney said that includes having the "right partners" among Arctic nations working together. "The phrase that always sticks with me ... is 'High North, low tension,'" he said.

The way to accomplish that, he said, includes submarine and space capacity.

AnalysisZelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters

In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.

Carney said the "time spent, whether it's in the high north in Norway, a meeting with the French president who's directly implicated in a number of these decisions, our meeting today and beyond, it's all connected."

Before his meeting with Støre in Ottawa, Carney travelled to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron earlier in the day.

Støre's visit comes as Carney looks for closer ties with Europe, including potential "associate membership" in the European Union.

Norway is not a member of the EU, but for three decades the country has had a deal with the political and economic bloc that gives both sides free access to each other's markets for goods and services — and gives Norway access to most EU programs.

Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.

Carney was in Norway in March — the first sitting Canadian prime minister since 1980 to visit the Nordic country.

During that visit, the two leaders pledged to advance collaboration in fields ranging from Arctic security and space to critical minerals and energy. Carney and Støre also touted their reputations as low-risk global oil producers, amid supply shocks emanating from conflicts like U.S. President Donald Trump's war on Iran.

AnalysisNo longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight

Norwegian officials have often described Canada as a similar country, given that both seek to balance a large oil sector with a push for green energy and respect for Indigenous people.

They both put an emphasis on using multilateral institutions to resolve disputes while identifying as strong proponents of NATO and deeply tied with the EU, without being members. Both countries have put support for Ukraine at the forefront of foreign policy, amid Russia's full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.

Since late 2024, Canada has had an Arctic foreign policy that calls for more intense ties with Nordic countries in defence, strategic sectors and environmental issues.
news.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive, petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.

news.title: Trump seeks to further tighten grip on biomedical research: US media
news.text:
WASHINGTON, United States: President Donald Trump is seeking to take control of American health research funding as part of his war against “woke” programs and institutions, US media reported over the weekend.

Since returning to power in early 2025, Trump has drastically cut federal funding for research, particularly in biomedicine.

White House officials have discussed the idea of creating an external commission capable of vetoing grants awarded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the US agency responsible for medical research, according to anonymous sources cited by media outlets including Politico, The New York Times and The Washington Post.

The White House budget director Russell Vought, a rightwing Trump loyalist, led the criticism, accusing the NIH of funding “woke” research, according to the Post.

In response to the reports, the president of non-profit alliance Research!America, Russ Paulsen, said in a statement Sunday that “adding more bureaucrats would slow medical progress to a grinding halt.”

“American patients and their families waiting for the next lifesaving treatment or medical breakthrough should not have to wait even longer,” he said.

Such a measure would allow the White House to further tighten its grip on scientific research, even as many critics have denounced the administration’s attacks on academic and research freedoms.

Harvard University and other top institutions, where much of the research takes place, are at the heart of Trump’s wider bid to impose his right-wing vision on US research and education.

Last week, American researchers filed a lawsuit against the NIH, accusing it of blocking grants in order to censor views it disagrees with, on everything from diversity and gender identity to climate change.

“Our study on Alzheimer’s disease was designed to better understand how to identify and reduce the risk of dementia in communities who are at high risk of developing the disease, who have been historically understudied,” Cohen said in a recent statement.

news.title: Iran blockade: US forces redirect 109 commercial vessels in Strait of Hormuz
news.text:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said its forces have redirected 109 commercial vessels amid a continued naval blockade on Iran from Washington, as heightened tensions around the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz disrupt regional shipping.

In a post on X on Sunday (local time), CENTCOM said the latest figure represented vessels redirected to ensure compliance with the US maritime blockade.

“A U.S. Sailor stands watch aboard USS John Paul Jones (DDG 53). As of Sept. 20, CENTCOM forces have redirected 109 commercial vessels to ensure total compliance,” CENTCOM said.

Strait of Hormuz shipping activity falls sharply

The US military resumed enforcement of the blockade against maritime traffic entering and exiting Iranian ports on July 14. CENTCOM has said the measures apply to vessels transiting to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas, while US forces continue to support traffic through regional waters for vessels not violating the blockade.

The latest development comes amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran, with the Strait of Hormuz at the centre of the confrontation. The waterway is a critical route for global energy shipments, and shipping activity has fallen sharply amid the conflict. Reuters reported that only four commodity vessels transited the strait on September 17, well below the 10-day average of 16.

Trump warns of ‘significant action’

US President Donald Trump on Sunday warned Iran that Washington could take ‘significant action’ if Tehran does not change its approach to the conflict, while also indicating that he could be open to diplomatic engagement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the UN General Assembly in New York.

Trump said he was in a decision-making phase over Iran and suggested that “very big things” could happen in the near future.

Iran conveys conditions for ending conflict

Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, meanwhile, said Tehran had conveyed conditions for ending the conflict through Qatari mediation. According to the statement cited in the briefings, Iran is seeking an end to hostilities on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the naval blockade.

“We remain in contact with the mediator Qatar, which has conveyed our conditions to Washington with the aim of ending the war,” Rezaei said, adding that Iran was awaiting Trump’s response.

Houthi attacks add to regional tensions

The maritime confrontation has also coincided with a fresh escalation involving Yemen’s Houthi movement. Houthi forces launched missile and drone attacks towards Saudi Arabia, including an attack directed at Riyadh that Saudi forces said was intercepted.

news.summary: Shipping through the strategically vital waterway has declined sharply as Washington and Tehran remain locked in an escalating confrontation over Iran

news.title: Medvedev accuses Europe of understanding “only the language of force” amid row over seized Western assets
news.text:
Kremlin security council deputy chief lashes out as France urges Moscow to reverse takeover of Auchan, Nestlé and Lemana Pro assets

Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Europe understood only the language of strength, in a pointed response to growing concern over the fate of European companies’ assets still operating in Russia.

France called on Moscow on Friday to reconsider its decision to take control of assets belonging to Auchan, Nestlé and Lemana Pro (formerly Leroy Merlin), a move the Kremlin justified on the grounds that the firms came from what it called “unfriendly countries.” Under a decree signed by President Vladimir Putin and published on Thursday, the companies’ assets are to be transferred “temporarily” to the Russian firm L.E.V. Management.

Writing on Telegram, Medvedev, a former Russian president and prime minister who now leads the governing United Russia party, said that today, as a century ago, he claimed European nations understood only naked force. He accused Western governments of effectively waging war against Russia by supplying Ukraine with weapons, including missiles, while simultaneously seeking to shield companies such as Nestlé and Auchan that continue to generate substantial profits in Russia.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the imposition of the first Western sanctions, numerous multinational companies have withdrawn from the Russian market, with the assets of some seized and subsequently transferred to Russian firms. A number of companies have nonetheless continued operating in Russia, drawing sharp criticism from Ukraine and other countries, which accuse them of effectively helping to finance the Russian state and its war effort.

Medvedev argued that the United States — where President Donald Trump signed into law on Friday new sanctions legislation targeting Russia over the war in Ukraine — should be treated no differently to Europe, saying those “on the other side of the ocean” also understood only the language of direct military deterrence. He said this was the register in which Russia needed to respond to what he called “Russophobic, repugnant actions,” citing the sanctions bill associated with the late US senator Lindsey Graham.

The legislation, the first major congressional initiative targeting Russia since Trump’s return to the presidency, is aimed primarily at Russia’s energy sector. It is named for its chief sponsor, Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July and had been one of the most vocal supporters of Ukraine and critics of Russia in the US Senate.
news.summary: Kremlin security council deputy chief lashes out as France urges Moscow to reverse takeover of Auchan, Nestlé and Lemana Pro…

news.title: US Warns of Rapid Escalation in West Asia War
news.text: RIYADH: The United States warned that fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis could "escalate rapidly" after a missile attack targeted Riyadh for the first time since the Yemen conflict resumed. US President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, a secluded presidential complex in rural Maryland, to return unexpectedly to the White House. The White House gave no explanation for the early return, which comes as a new threshold was crossed in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen and are fighting government forces backed by a coalition led by Riyadh. Loud explosions rang out on Saturday in the Saudi capital, where AFP journalists saw a fuel tank bearing the logo of oil giant Aramco on fire near the airport. "This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," the US State Department warned, adding American citizens outside the Middle East should "seriously reconsider travel to and through the region". Separately, the State Department restricted travel for American government employees to the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu, home to a major Red Sea oil export terminal that has previously been targeted by Houthi strikes. In recent weeks, the Houthis' lightning offensive seizing swathes of Yemeni territory has left hundreds dead and, according to the UN refugee agency, displaced more than 110,000 people. - 'Intercepted' - The violence has already disrupted exports from Saudi Arabia, the world's leading supplier of crude oil, as well as maritime traffic. Saudi Arabia's ally the United States has sent mixed signals. According to US news platform Axios, Washington refused last week a Saudi request to strike the Houthis, and Fox News reported Sunday that Trump had said the Houthis have agreed not to hit US targets. On Sunday, US Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in a rare visit to Cairo. The visit came days after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was also in the Egyptian capital, where he and Sisi urged safe and secure navigation through Bab al-Mandab, after the Houthis seized the Yemeni coast. The Bab al-Mandab strait is a Red Sea waterway that is crucial to energy flows and global shipping and which has become even more strategic since Iran imposed a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Condemning the Houthis' latest attacks, Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told the broadcaster NTV that his country had discussions with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, partners in a mutual defence pact, about possible assistance. "In this regard, military needs, especially in state technical matters, may happen. There would be no problem in meeting this demand either," he said. Saudi Arabia meanwhile has scrambled to contain the fallout of the Houthis' attacks on its territory. On Sunday, the attack on Riyadh was not mentioned in several major Saudi papers, even though hours beforehand, the Riyadh-led coalition had confirmed that a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis was "successfully intercepted and destroyed". The coalition added that the pro-Iranian fighters had tried to target "civilians and civilian infrastructure" in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil. Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but has failed to stop the fighters' advance in Yemen. Claiming responsibility for the attack, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said fighters had carried out "two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones". "The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu." - Lightning offensive - According to Andreas Krieg of King's College London, the attack on Riyadh, the first to threaten the Saudi capital since Yemen's civil war resumed, crossed "an important psychological threshold". "Saudi Arabia can absorb intermittent attacks on remote military or energy installations more easily than repeated threats to Riyadh itself," he told AFP. "Strikes around airports, fuel storage and populated areas make restraint politically and strategically much harder to sustain." The attack has piled further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war in the Middle East, which began in February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran and which has seen the Islamic republic respond with attacks around the region. Iran-backed groups also got involved, with Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen carrying out attacks against their foes. news.title: Macron, Carney meet to reaffirm France-Canada ties after Trump's map row
news.text:
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pledged closer cooperation on energy, security and climate change during a meeting on the French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon on Sunday.
The meeting came as both countries face growing geopolitical tensions and trade pressures from the United States under President Donald Trump.
The visit to the small North Atlantic archipelago carried significant symbolic weight. It was Macron's first visit to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon since 2014 and the first-ever visit by a Canadian prime minister to the French territory.
The meeting also came weeks after Trump shared a social media post showing a map of North America, including Canada, Greenland and French territories such as Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, covered by the US flag and labelled 'United States of America'.
Asked about the post during a joint press conference, Macron dismissed any suggestion that the islands' status was in question. He said there was no need to repeatedly reaffirm French sovereignty in response to what he described as 'strange ideas'.
À Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon pour ouvrir une nouvelle page d’avenir. pic.twitter.com/7P51XLanRR
— Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) September 20, 2026
Macron, Carney call for closer ties
The meeting reflected growing efforts by Canada and France to strengthen their partnership as geopolitical tensions rise and protectionism increases.
Carney said the two countries were facing a number of common challenges, including climate change, threats to sovereignty and what he described as the erosion of democratic norms.
'Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to our sovereignty,' Carney said alongside Macron.
'The time has come to strengthen our ties,' he added.
Macron said France and Canada shared a commitment to multilateralism, the rule of law and greater strategic autonomy.
'We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so,' Macron said.
Canada has increasingly looked towards Europe as it seeks to diversify its economic and strategic partnerships. The European Union has also opened the door for Canada to become its first associate member, a move strongly supported by France.
Energy, critical minerals on agenda
Energy security was another key focus of the talks.
France has been pushing for greater Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe as European countries seek to strengthen their energy security and reduce exposure to supply disruptions.
'Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,' Macron said.
The two countries also discussed potential cooperation in areas including critical minerals, rare earths, aerospace and advanced technologies such as quantum computing.
However, closer economic ties between Canada and the EU still face hurdles. The Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA, between the two sides was signed more than a decade ago but has yet to be fully ratified by all EU member states, including France.
Why Saint-Pierre and Miquelon matters
Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is a small French territory located off Canada's Newfoundland coast. Its location gives it particular strategic significance, sitting at the intersection of French, Canadian and wider North Atlantic interests.
For Macron and Carney, the meeting was a chance to strengthen France-Canada ties and work more closely amid growing global tensions.
Macron will travel to New York after the visit to attend the United Nations General Assembly, where global security, sovereignty and transatlantic relations are expected to be key issues.

news.title: World News | US Issues Iran Travel Warning, Urges Citizens to Leave Country Amid Rising West Asia Tensions
news.text:
Tehran [Iran], September 21 (ANI): The United States has issued a fresh travel warning for Iran, urging American citizens not to travel to the country “for any reason” and asking those already there to leave immediately amid rising tensions and the possibility of further escalation across West Asia.

The US Virtual Embassy in Iran, in a security alert, said the regional security environment remained complex and warned of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says He's in 'Deciding Mode' on Iran, Warns of 'Very Big Things' As Tehran Sends 7 Conditions.

“Do not travel to Iran for any reason. U.S. citizens should leave Iran now,” the alert said.

The US Mission urged Americans currently in the region to exercise heightened vigilance and closely monitor developments affecting airports, airlines and border crossings.

Also Read | How People in China Are Licensing Their Faces to AI for up to INR 14 Lakh.

It also warned that procedures at Iran's land borders could change with little notice and advised travellers to check the entry requirements of countries they may seek to enter.

The alert comes amid an escalating confrontation involving the United States and Iran, with Washington maintaining military and maritime pressure on Tehran and Iranian officials warning of retaliation against US interests in the region.

The US also cited the activities of Iranian-supported Houthi forces, which have carried out attacks against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports.

“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the alert said.

The United States further warned that its diplomatic facilities, including locations outside the Middle East, have previously been targeted and that Iran or groups supportive of Tehran could target US interests, businesses and institutions overseas.

American citizens were advised to enrol in the Department of State's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and facilitate contact with US diplomatic authorities during emergencies.

The alert also advised citizens to avoid demonstrations, large gatherings and areas with heavy police presence, while maintaining a low profile at locations publicly associated with the United States.

In case of an aerial attack, Americans were instructed to stay away from windows and glass doors, avoid fallen debris and monitor official communications.

The latest warning follows a separate US security alert for Americans and US government personnel in Saudi Arabia. The US Mission in Saudi Arabia recently required government employees to obtain special authorisation for official and personal travel to Taif and Yanbu amid heightened security concerns following Houthi attacks.

Saudi authorities had issued an emergency warning over a “hostile aerial threat” after a ballistic missile was launched towards Riyadh. Saudi-led coalition forces said the missile was intercepted and also reported attempted attacks targeting civilian populations and infrastructure in Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu.

Qatar has condemned the Houthi attacks and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, describing the strikes as a violation of the kingdom's sovereignty and international law.

The US State Department has separately urged Americans travelling to or through West Asia to remain vigilant as regional tensions raise the risk of sudden flight disruptions, airspace closures and attacks targeting US interests. (ANI)

news.text: Washington: President Donald Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when Trump travels to the city for the upcoming UN General Assembly.The meeting is scheduled for Monday at Gracie Mansion, the official mayoral residence, according to Anna Bahr, Mamdani's communications director.Bahr said the two will discuss issues affecting the city and New Yorkers. news.title: Houthis Assure Trump US Ships Won’t Be Targeted, Warn Others Against Joining Saudi Arabia
news.text:
The Iran-backed Houthis have told the Donald Trump administration that they will not target US vessels in the Red Sea, while warning other countries against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen’s escalating conflict.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told The Associated Press that Washington reached out to the group after its rapid advance along Yemen’s western coast towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait earlier this month. He said the Houthis assured US officials that their operations were not directed at the United States or other countries using the strategic waterway.
“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” al-Bukhaiti said in an interview from Sanaa.
Trump had revealed days earlier that his administration had held discussions with the Houthis. “The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us,” Trump said last weekend, adding that the group wanted to avoid US involvement and was allowing most ships to pass through.
ALSO READ | 'When Do I Blow Entire Nation?': Trump Says 3 Options On Table For Iran
Houthis Say Bab el-Mandeb Will Remain Open
According to an AP report, Oman hosted talks between US and Houthi representatives last weekend. While al-Bukhaiti did not confirm direct negotiations, he acknowledged indirect contacts through Oman, which brokered a ceasefire between the Houthis and the Trump administration in 2025.
That agreement ended a week-long US bombing campaign after the rebels agreed to halt attacks on US vessels in the Red Sea. Al-Bukhaiti also insisted that the Houthis were not seeking to shut the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
“The goal of our military operations is not to close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but rather to ensure freedom of navigation through it for everyone, including Yemen,” he said.
At the same time, al-Bukhaiti warned that the Houthis were prepared to widen the conflict if additional countries joined Saudi Arabia’s campaign.
“Today, Yemen is capable of waging battle — not merely an internal conflict, but an international one as well,” he said.
ALSO READ | Ed Sheeran Calls Gaza War 'Catastrophic, Unjustifiable' Amid Macklemore Tour Controversy
Houthis Demand End To Saudi Blockade
Al-Bukhaiti said attacks on Saudi Arabia would continue until Riyadh lifted its decade-long blockade on rebel-held territories and allowed ships to access Houthi-controlled Red Sea ports. He said the group would then be prepared to negotiate.
The Houthi official blamed Saudi Arabia for the latest escalation, saying the renewed fighting followed an airstrike attributed to the Saudi-led coalition that struck Sanaa International Airport and prevented an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. He said the flight was intended to challenge the coalition’s air and naval blockade.
The Houthis subsequently launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi targets, including a strike aimed at Riyadh on Saturday that was intercepted. Saudi authorities said debris from a Houthi drone killed one civilian and wounded others.
The rebels have also announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea. They have targeted Saudi-linked vessels and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom.

news.title: 'Peace track our number one priority': Zelensky says Trump meeting could change a lot
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 21 (IANS) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that he and US President Donald Trump had agreed to meet in New York, and said Ukraine was ready to take serious steps towards peace in coordination with the American team. “We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelensky said in a post on X after speaking with Trump. He did not announce a date for the meeting or specify what the two leaders hoped to agree. His account outlined areas under discussion but did not announce a peace agreement or a timetable for implementing any measures. Zelensky described the conversation as important and said it had covered substantial ground. He placed the pursuit of peace at the centre of Ukraine’s engagement with the American team. “The peace track is our number one priority,” he said. The Ukrainian president identified energy security, food security and the protection of human life as issues being considered alongside possible steps to reduce tensions. He did not set out the individual proposals or explain how they would be put into practice. “There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life,” he said. Zelensky also signalled Ukraine’s willingness to act, saying work with US officials was continuing. “We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps,” he said. He did not identify those steps or say whether they would require reciprocal action. The post did not set out any commitments by Russia. Zelensky thanked Trump for a visit to Kyiv by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said the visit had allowed detailed discussions and given the two Americans a direct view of conditions in Ukraine. “We went through the key details thoroughly, and they saw the situation in Ukraine firsthand,” he said. Separately, Zelensky thanked the US president for signing legislation he referred to as the Lindsey Graham bill into law. “I thanked the American President for signing the Lindsey Graham bill into law,” he said. The post did not give the legislation’s formal title, describe its provisions or explain how it related to the diplomatic steps under discussion. “We all concur – there must be peace. Thank you to everyone who stands with Ukraine! Thank you to everyone who’s helping!” he said.

news.title: World News | Russia State Duma Polls: Putin-backed United Russia Leads Parliamentary Polls with 57.5% Amid Ukrainian Strikes
news.text:
Moscow [Russia], September 21 (ANI): Russia's ruling United Russia party, which backs President Vladimir Putin, is leading the country's State Duma elections with 57.5 per cent of the vote, according to initial results, as the parliamentary polls were held against the backdrop of the ongoing war in Ukraine.

According to CNN, final results are not expected before September 25. Initial data from Russia's Central Election Commission showed United Russia comfortably ahead after the three-day voting process ended on Sunday.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says He's in 'Deciding Mode' on Iran, Warns of 'Very Big Things' As Tehran Sends 7 Conditions.

The election is the first State Duma vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Putin has presented the election as an indication of public support for the country's military and political course.

“Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together, united by shared values, our historical memory, love for our Motherland,” Putin said ahead of the vote, according to CNN.

Also Read | How People in China Are Licensing Their Faces to AI for up to INR 14 Lakh.

The elections were held amid a tightly controlled political environment, with CNN reporting that meaningful opposition to the Kremlin was largely absent. Russia's only registered anti-war party, Yabloko, was barred from participating in the federal party-list election by the Supreme Court last month.

Putin himself was not on the ballot. He is not due to face a presidential election until 2030. United Russia won 324 of the 450 seats in the State Duma in the previous parliamentary elections in 2021.

The election also coincided with heightened military activity between Russia and Ukraine. CNN reported that Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones towards Moscow and the surrounding region on Sunday, with Russian officials saying the attacks killed at least two people and damaged a major oil refinery.

The attacks came as Russia's parliamentary vote entered its final day. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said the strikes had been planned to disrupt the elections, a claim that Ukraine did not independently confirm.

Voter turnout is also being closely watched. According to the Central Election Commission, overall turnout stood at 56.66 per cent, while Moscow recorded high participation.

CNN reported that the outcome was widely expected given the absence of credible opposition, making turnout and the eventual distribution of the 450 Duma seats key indicators of the political environment.

The Kremlin is expected to use the election outcome to demonstrate domestic backing for Putin and his policies, including the military campaign in Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Russian citizens abroad also participated in the three-day voting process. In India, Russian Ambassador Denis Alipov cast his ballot in New Delhi, where polling facilities were established for Russian citizens in the country. Five polling stations were set up across India, including in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Goa.

The results are expected to be finalised by September 25, after which the composition of Russia's next State Duma will become clearer. (ANI)

news.title: World News | “This is a Disgrace”: Imran Khan’s Son Kasim Alleges Relatives Arrested Ahead of PTI March
news.text:
Lahore [Pakistan], September 21 (ANI): Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan’s son Kasim Khan has alleged that some of his relatives, including his aunts and cousins, have been arrested with no information provided about their whereabouts, days ahead of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) planned protest march on September 27.

Kasim, in a series of posts on X, alleged that his aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with cousins Shershah and Shahrez, had been taken into custody after authorities entered their homes and forced them into vehicles.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says He's in 'Deciding Mode' on Iran, Warns of 'Very Big Things' As Tehran Sends 7 Conditions.

“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noureen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez have now been abducted as well,” Kasim said.

“They have broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he alleged.

Also Read | How People in China Are Licensing Their Faces to AI for up to INR 14 Lakh.

Kasim described the alleged arrests as “criminal behaviour” and called for international attention to the situation.

In another post, he claimed that Shahrez's two children, aged four and six, were initially missing. He later said the children were safe, but alleged that two more cousins, Azeem and Sakeenah, had been arrested.

“Hearing news that my cousin’s children are now safe. Meanwhile, two more of my cousins have been arrested. Azeem and Sakeenah. No reasons given. No location given,” he said.

The allegations come after Imran Khan’s sister Aleema Khan was detained in Lahore under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) law ahead of PTI's planned September 27 protest march. Lahore Deputy Commissioner Muhammad Ali Ijaz ordered her detention for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960.

According to Dawn, police confirmed that Aleema was taken to Kot Lakhpat jail. The detention order cited concerns over public safety and maintenance of public order, while alleging her involvement in protests and roadblocks and mobilisation of PTI workers.

PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan condemned Aleema’s detention and demanded her release, arguing that the move could increase tensions ahead of the planned protest.

Aleema’s son Shahrez Khan had earlier alleged that his mother was “abducted” after leaving her home and said the family had no contact or information about her whereabouts.

The September 27 PTI march is being organised to demand the release of Imran Khan, who remains incarcerated and faces multiple legal cases. 

Meanwhile, according to authorities, Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up in jail amid continuing concerns surrounding his physical well-being, according to Pakistani media reports.

Authorities have cited public-order concerns for Aleema Khan’s detention, while PTI and members of Khan’s family have challenged the arrests and demanded information about the whereabouts of those taken into custody. (ANI)

news.title: Ukraine fires new homemade Pelican ballistic missile in largest attack on Moscow yet - as fears grow across Europe that Putin is preparing to attack
news.text:
Ukraine fires new homemade Pelican ballistic missile in largest attack on Moscow yet - as fears grow across Europe that Putin is preparing to attack

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

By WILL HALLOWELL, NEWS REPORTER and SABRINA PENTY, FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER

Published: 01:33 BST, 21 September 2026 | Updated: 01:34 BST, 21 September 2026

Ukraine has fired a new homemade ballistic missile at Russia in the country's largest attack on Moscow since the start of the war. 

On Sunday night, the final day of the Russian election, Ukraine struck an oil refinery on the outskirts of the capital as Volodymyr Zelensky hailed the 'strength' of Kyiv's 'long-range capabilities' after Pelican's involvement in the attack. 

Pelican refers to the FP-7 ground-launched ballistic missile that was developed in Ukraine by defence technology company Fire Point, The Telegraph reports.

Fire Point is a Ukrainian firm that develops UAV and missile systems for 'modern precision warfare'. 

FP-7 completed testing earlier this month and its involvement in last night's oil refinery bombardment marks the new system's first publicly confirmed combat deployment. 

The missiles have a maximum range of 200km (124 miles) with an accuracy of 13m.

But it comes amid growing fears across Europe that Vladimir Putin is preparing to attack Nato territory. 

Sharing footage of the attack from Sunday night, Mr Zelensky said in a social media post: 'Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. 

Plumes of smoke rise from fires (right) at an oil refinery following what the authorities say is a Ukrainian drone strike in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, in Moscow, Russia, September, 20, 2026

Smoke blankets Moscow following a strike on an oil refinery 

The latest Ukrainian strikes started fires across the Moscow region 

'One of Russia's key oil industry facilities and the aggressor's logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine. 

'The systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen, and Pelican.'

He added: 'I thank everyone who is strengthening Ukraine's long-range capabilities.'

Meanwhile, Ukraine appears to be scaling up its use of ballistic missiles as Fire Point's CEO Iryna Terekh said on September 10 during a speech at a defence conference that a longer ranged FP-9 system was 'currently undergoing flight tests'. 

The mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, claimed Russia had come under attack from more than 1,600 drones on Sunday and accused Ukraine of attempting to 'disrupt' the elections. 

He added that 450 drones targeting the city were shot down but said a number of them reached the oil refinery, with one destroying a nearby apartment. 

Huge fires burned through Moscow overnight following one of Ukraine's largest drone attacks on the Russian capital.

Two people were killed as Ukraine and Russia continue to attack each other's energy infrastructure – despite an announcement by US President Donald Trump on Monday that they had agreed ⁠to stop.

Volodymyr Zelensky thanked defence partners for 'strengthening Ukraine's long-range capabilities'

Two people were killed in the latest attack

A view shows a damaged multi-storey apartment building following a drone attack in Kotelniki in the Moscow region on September 20, 2026

People gather outside a damaged residential building following what authorities described as a Ukrainian drone strike, amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Sofyino settlement in the Ramensky district of the Moscow region, Russia, September, 20, 2026

Ukraine's Pelican deployment on Sunday comes amid growing fears that Mr Putin could be planning to launch attacks on Nato countries. 

European spy chiefs have issued a chilling warning that Russia could be just months away from dramatically escalating its campaign against Nato – potentially through missile or drone attacks, sabotage or even a limited incursion onto alliance territory.

Senior intelligence officials across the continent are increasingly concerned that Moscow could soon attempt to deliberately test Nato's resolve, with one security chief warning that the danger could materialise in a matter of 'months, not years'.

The alarming assessment comes as European governments grapple with what they say is a growing campaign of Russian sabotage and provocation designed to frighten populations, fracture the alliance and weaken support for Ukraine.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has told lawmakers that intelligence assessments suggest Russia could launch drones or missiles at Nato territory in the coming months in an attempt to demonstrate that the alliance's crucial Article 5 mutual-defence guarantee is 'more theoretical than practical'.

French President Emmanuel Macron described Mr Tusk's warning as 'sound and well-documented' and on Friday summoned political party leaders and candidates for France's 2027 presidential election to an emergency meeting in Paris, where Russia's growing threat was among the subjects discussed.

But one of the starkest warnings came from Michal Koudelka, who heads the Czech Republic's BIS security service.

Mr Koudelka told The Guardian that Moscow's next move could go beyond the increased drone activity already unnerving European capitals and potentially involve a small-scale incursion into Nato territory bordering Russia.

'It's possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,' he said in a rare interview at the agency's Prague headquarters.

Asked about the potential timeframe, Mr Koudelka said such a scenario could unfold in 'months, not years', although he stressed that 'a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn't happen'.

The warning comes amid a dangerous period in Russia's war against Ukraine, with both Moscow and Kyiv intensifying their long-range attacks.

Meanwhile the head of Latvia's state security service, the VDD, Normunds Mežviets, said: 'It's still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it's just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society.'

But he told the newspaper that 'we don't see indications of an imminent attack'. 

And secretary general of Estonia's foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov said there has been 'panic on social media' in recent days over the possibility of a Russian attack. 

He added that until there is 'reason to fear an attack', people should 'keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine'. 

The latest attack from Ukraine comes as Russia entered its third and final day of a parliamentary election that Mr Putin has cast as a test of support for his country's war in Ukraine.

'The unprecedented attack ​was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections,' Sobyanin said. 'The adversary ​failed to achieve this.'

A major warehouse in a logistics hub in the nearby town of Sofyino was also struck, killing a woman and injuring five others – including two children. 

Elsewhere in the Orekhovo-Zuyevsky district, an elderly man was killed by a downed drone.

Images showed how thick black smoke blanketed part of the city as it billowed from the site of the Moscow refinery.

The scale of any damage to the facility was not immediately known, while all four of Moscow's main airports faced major disruption as the capital's airspace was closed.

Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia's oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country's ⁠11 time zones.

The Moscow plant, which has been targeted multiple times, processed 11.6 million metric tons of oil in 2024, producing 2.9 million tons of gasoline and 3.2 million tons of diesel, the ⁠latest available data shows.

Ukraine has not commented on the attacks and both sides say they do not target civilians.

In the wider Moscow region, in addition to the two deaths, ⁠400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-storey apartment block in the Ramenskoye district, and many homes were damaged, said Governor Andrei Vorobyov.

Russia's electoral chief said on Sunday that there had been over 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks targeting Russian election infrastructure in recent days.

DDoS attacks involve overwhelming a system with internet traffic so that it is unable to function normally.

'Over the past period, more than 1,000 waves of DDoS attacks have been recorded against infrastructure in Russia that is specifically involved in the electoral process,' the chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, Ella Pamfilova, was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies.

Russians began three days of voting on Friday in the country's first wartime parliamentary election.

The State Duma vote is expected to see the ruling United Russia party easily retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.

The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Mr Putin's policies and for the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since the Second World War, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.

Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot.

Russian President Vladimir Putin votes online in the parliamentary election in Moscow, Russia, September 18, 2026

Citizens cast their ballots at a polling station in Moscow, Russia, on September 19, 2026, during the country's parliamentary elections

Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities.

Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.

In a small act of defiance, Yabloko's leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstratively spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party's name and the slogan 'For peace'.

The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military ⁠operation in Ukraine.

It casts the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.

Russian electoral officials said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyber-attack.

Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a 'pseudo election'. 

However, Russia's ruling party that supports Vladimir Putin is set for a landslide victory in the country's first wartime parliamentary elections, widely regarded as a 'sham'.

The pro-war United Russia party is projected by early counting to take around 58 per cent of the vote, with its closest rival the Communist Party on track for just 14 per cent.

Polls closed to the 111 million-strong electorate on Sunday just hours after Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones into Russia, including an 'unprecedented' number at the capital Moscow.

Voting stretched to Russian-held areas of Ukraine, prompting Kyiv to urge foreign governments against recognising the outcome.

Mr Putin was not on the ballot paper because these elections were for the state Duma – Russia's parliament – rather than the presidential seat. 

He is also not a member of United Russia, but he served as its leader between 2008 and 2012.

The current leader is Mr Putin's ally, former president and prime minister Dmitry Medvedev.

He has already vowed to implement the dictator's will in the new parliament.

The result of the election – which ran across three days at a turnout of 56 per cent – was never truly in doubt because the Kremlin exerts tight control over the voting process.

They are broadly similar to the results of the last election in 2021, despite growing unease over the war among civilians.

Russian elections have for decades been marred by corruption allegations, and this year's was no different.

Members of a local electoral commission count the ballots at the end of parliamentary elections at a polling station in Podolsk, Moscow region

A man casts his ballot during voting at a polling station

Evidence emerged that some ballots had been pre-marked to force votes of United Russia. 

There were also reports of ballot stuffing, where a voter casts more than their one permitted paper.

Credible opposition is virtually non-existent in Russia, with critics of the current regime barred, jailed or exiled – particularly if they begin to gain political traction.

Human rights groups estimate more than 2,000 people are currently locked up for political reasons.

Russia's only overtly anti-war party Yabloko – meaning Apple – had been banned from standing to prevent any criticism of Mr Putin's military policy, but some of its candidates contested individual constituencies.

Voting was also organised in war-torn regions of Ukraine that have been invaded by Russia since the outbreak of war in February 2022.

In the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, election officials reported 82 per cent, with similarly high figures in the Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.

The European Union on Friday called the action a 'blatant violation of international law'.

news.title: World News | Trump to Meet Zelenskyy in New York on Tuesday as US Pushes for Russia-Ukraine De-escalation Deal
news.text:
Washington DC [US], September 21 (ANI): US President Donald Trump is set to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on Tuesday as the United States pushes efforts to secure de-escalation between Russia and Ukraine, with the two leaders expected to discuss steps towards reducing hostilities and reviving negotiations.

The meeting is being organised on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. According to Axios, Ukrainian chief negotiator Rustem Umerov, who also heads Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, has been working with White House envoys in to arrange the talks.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says He's in 'Deciding Mode' on Iran, Warns of 'Very Big Things' As Tehran Sends 7 Conditions.

The planned meeting follows a phone conversation between Trump and Zelenskyy, during which the two leaders agreed to meet in New York.

Zelenskyy described the conversation as important and said it had generated diplomatic momentum.

Also Read | How People in China Are Licensing Their Faces to AI for up to INR 14 Lakh.

“I just spoke with President Trump. An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

According to Axios, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy during the call to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, with the attacks being linked to disruptions in fuel supplies and higher diesel prices. A source familiar with the conversation told Axios that “the word diesel came up many times during the call.”

The issue of energy infrastructure has emerged as an important element of US efforts to reduce tensions between Moscow and Kyiv. Zelenskyy has previously indicated that Ukraine could halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Russia provides firm guarantees against attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure.

Zelenskyy also thanked Trump for sending US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv, saying they had reviewed key issues and seen the situation in Ukraine firsthand.

“The peace track is our number one priority,” Zelenskyy said, adding that discussions were underway on possible de-escalation measures and security issues involving energy, food and the protection of human life.

The New York meeting comes as the war continues to intensify, with Russia and Ukraine carrying out long-range attacks despite diplomatic efforts.

US officials have been exploring possible short-term de-escalation measures while seeking to restart broader negotiations aimed at ending the conflict. Axios previously reported that Washington was examining the possibility of winter de-escalation steps between Russia and Ukraine as part of efforts to revive negotiations.

The talks will take place as world leaders gather in New York for the 81st UN General Assembly, with the Ukraine conflict expected to remain among the major issues discussed during the high-level week. (ANI)

news.title: Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror Vows to Speak Out as Lawyer Warns of Public Attacks
news.text:
The sole juror who prevented a verdict in Lindsay Clancy’s triple-murder trial plans to explain his position in his own words. His attorney says jurors must be free to follow the evidence without fearing public retaliation.

Attorney Edward Paltzik said Michael P. Desronvil, whose decision not to join the other jurors resulted in a mistrial, will release a personal statement “in the near future.”

“Michael will be making a personal statement in the near future, in his own words,” Paltzik wrote in a Facebook post.

Paltzik expressed gratitude to people who sent Desronvil supportive emails, text messages and voice recordings, while recognizing that some observers may disagree with the stance he took during deliberations.

“This country was built on intelligent debate in the public square,” Paltzik wrote. “That’s the same reason we support the good faith right of an individual juror to follow the evidence and the law to wherever they take him or her, free from fear of reprisal.”

The comments come as the sharply divided case returns to national attention. Patrick Clancy, the father of the three children and Lindsay Clancy’s former husband, gave his first television interview Sunday on CBS News’ “60 Minutes.”

Patrick Clancy spoke about his grief, his memories of the children and baseless conspiracy theories that have circulated online since the killings in January 2023. His wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, also appeared in the segment alongside correspondent Ross Douthat.

Lindsay Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. The children were found strangled inside the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023.

Clancy acknowledged killing the children, but her lawyers argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that the former labor and delivery nurse understood her actions and carried out the killings intentionally.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, following seven days of deliberations. The jury stood at 11-1: Eleven jurors were prepared to find Clancy not criminally responsible, while Desronvil continued to advocate for a conviction.

Desronvil later said he was convinced that prosecutors had proved their case.

“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” Desronvil said in a statement first reported by NewsNation and confirmed to News Outlet by Paltzik.

Desronvil said he introduced several theories during deliberations, but fellow jurors repeatedly interrupted him and interpreted his questions as signs of uncertainty.

The mistrial’s repercussions soon extended beyond the courtroom, as Desronvil faced intense public scrutiny for refusing to change his position.

Paltzik, who previously represented President Donald Trump in lawsuits against The New York Times, CBS and ABC News, told News Outlet that his priority is Desronvil’s “health, safety and well-being.” He has described the juror as an “American Hero” and “Champion of Justice.”

Former prosecutor and behavioral health law expert Mark Astor previously told News Outlet that Desronvil appeared to have hired counsel to defend his name after being “dragged through the mud.”

“The whole idea of the jury is sort of this sacred arena where jurors get to decide a verdict in a case,” Astor said. “And now we’re taking what is really a sacred arena, and we’re exposing it to the public.”

Plymouth County prosecutors have not announced whether they will retry Clancy. Her defense team has raised the possibility of resolving the case without another trial and brought in veteran Boston attorney Martin Weinberg to pursue a motion seeking dismissal on double-jeopardy grounds.

Clancy is due back in Plymouth Superior Court for a status hearing Sept. 29, when the path forward could become clearer.

news.title: US, China start high-level talks on trade and AI ahead of Trump-Xi summit
news.text:
US and Chinese officials have begun high-level talks in New York, just days before US President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng began the talks on Sunday. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is also part of the discussions.
The talks are aimed at preparing the ground for the Trump-Xi meeting later this week, with trade, artificial intelligence and critical minerals among the key issues.
The two sides are also discussing the future of their fragile trade truce, which is due to expire in November.
Trade truce under focus
The trade truce is one of the most important issues on the table.
The agreement helped bring down tariffs after a major escalation in the US-China trade dispute. Both countries now face a decision on whether to extend the arrangement as the November expiry approaches.
Washington and Beijing have also been working to reduce trade barriers on selected goods.
Earlier negotiations included efforts to increase Chinese purchases of US agricultural products. The implementation of those commitments could also come under discussion during the latest talks.
Rare earths remain a key issue
The supply of rare earth magnets and other critical minerals is another major concern for the US.
These materials are widely used in industries such as automobiles, electronics and advanced manufacturing.
China had agreed to restore the flow of critical minerals under the earlier trade truce. US officials, however, have said that Beijing's performance has not been sufficient.
The issue has added another layer to the wider economic and technology competition between Washington and Beijing.
AI enters US-China negotiations
Artificial intelligence has become a new area of discussion between the two countries.
US officials have proposed talks on AI safeguards and ways to manage risks associated with increasingly powerful AI systems.
Bessent has said the US is open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and preventing the two countries from developing completely separate AI systems.
The discussions could cover both open-weight and closed-weight AI models. Chinese open-weight models have gained attention among US companies because they can be cheaper than some US-developed systems.
AI has also become part of the broader US-China technology rivalry, with Washington raising concerns about China's development of advanced AI capabilities.
Trump-Xi summit ahead
The New York talks come four days before Trump is expected to host Xi at the White House.
The meeting will be the next major engagement between the leaders of the world's two largest economies as both sides try to manage tensions over trade, technology and supply chains.
The immediate focus of the officials' talks is likely to be on areas where the two countries can keep tensions from rising further.
A major breakthrough is not expected from the negotiations, according to analysts cited in the source material. The more immediate objective is to maintain the existing trade truce and find limited areas of agreement.

news.title: Trump to meet with NYC lefty mayor Mamdani during UN General Assembly amid Netanyahu controversy
news.text:
President Donald Trump will make a trip to Gracie Mansion on Monday for a face-to-face meeting with New York City's democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Trump's visit comes as world leaders descend on Manhattan for the United Nations General Assembly and includes a visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu which threatens to inflame tensions across the city.

The political frenemies will sit down at the mayor's official Upper East Side residence during Trump's trip to New York marking their third known in-person meeting, but their first in New York.

City Hall offered few clues on Sunday about what exactly will be on the table.

'The meeting will focus on issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers,' Mamdani's office said.

The White House also confirmed the meeting but offered no additional details, while no time has publicly been announced.

The encounter comes during a politically charged week in New York, where the annual gathering of world leaders will again transform Manhattan into a fortress of road closures, motorcades and heavy security.

Trump is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Tuesday as part of a packed diplomatic schedule that includes meetings with several foreign leaders.

But the arrival of Netanyahu threatens to present Mamdani with a particularly delicate challenge.

Mamdani has spent years fiercely criticizing Netanyahu and Israel's conduct in Gaza.

Last week the mayor said that he does not plan to join protests surrounding the gathering and that the NYPD was preparing for the event.

Mamdani previously called Netanyahu a 'war criminal' and said he believed the Israeli prime minister 'belongs in The Hague,' referring to the International Criminal Court.

The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity connected to the Gaza conflict. 

Netanyahu and Israel have rejected the allegations, and Israel is not a member of the ICC.

Mamdani also vowed during his mayoral campaign that Netanyahu would face arrest if he came to New York, but subsequently acknowledged the legal constraints facing City Hall.

The United States is also not a party to the Rome Statute establishing the ICC, and the Trump administration has fiercely opposed the court's actions against Israeli officials.

The administration is now preparing broader sanctions against the ICC over its pursuit of Netanyahu, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Mamdani himself was coy last week when asked whether he would sit down with Trump while the president was in town.

'When it comes to the president, we continue to have a conversation about how best to deliver for this city,' he said.

'That is a conversation that has been done in person, it's been done over the phone, and it will continue so long as either of us have the ability to deliver for the city.'

For two politicians separated by enormous ideological differences, their relationship has repeatedly proved warmer than many expected.

During the 2025 mayoral campaign, Trump called Mamdani a '100% Communist Lunatic,' while Mamdani positioned himself as a determined opponent of the president's agenda.

Yet when Mamdani traveled to the White House after winning the election, their first encounter produced a surprisingly cordial display.

Trump even suggested the mayor-elect could 'surprise some conservative people.'

'We have one thing in common,' Trump said following that November meeting. 'We want this city of ours that we love to do very well.'

Mamdani returned to the White House in February for another private sit-down, where housing was among the issues discussed.
news.summary: President Donald Trump will meet NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Gracie Mansion on Monday as world leaders gather for the UN General Assembly.

news.title: Hyperliquid Just Hit a New All-Time High of $92. How Hyped Should Investors Be For HYPE?
news.text:
It's easy to see why crypto investors are so excited about Hyperliquid (HYPE +1.85%). For the year, it's up a resounding 260% and now ranks among the top 10 cryptocurrencies in the world by market cap. Even better, the HYPE token recently hit a new all-time high of $92 on Sept. 18.

To put that into context, Bitcoin still trades at a steep 36% discount to its all-time high of $126,000 in October. It now looks unlikely to reclaim the $100,000 level by the end of the year.

On the surface, then, Hyperliquid and Bitcoin appear to be headed in very different directions. Is it really the case that you should forget about Bitcoin and buy Hyperliquid instead?

The perpetual futures market is getting crowded

Hyperliquid is a decentralized cryptocurrency exchange that has skyrocketed in popularity, largely due to its ability to offer perpetual futures contracts to risk-seeking crypto traders.

These perpetual futures (known as "perps") allow for massive leverage, which helps amplify overall returns. Moreover, they enable traders to bet on both the upward and downward movement of a specific cryptocurrency, so you can (theoretically) make money in both bear and bull markets.

Until mid-2026, these perpetual futures were largely banned in the U.S. market due to their perceived risk. That changed at the end of May, when the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) gave the green light for trading in perpetual futures.

Immediately, prediction market Kalshi jumped into the fray. In addition to Bitcoin, it now offers perpetual futures contracts on 17 other cryptocurrencies (including Hyperliquid). As can be imagined, they were a hit from Day 1.

Now, plenty of other competitors want in on the action. Two of the most prominent names include Robinhood Markets and Coinbase Global. This makes me think that the perpetual futures market is getting too crowded.

Hyperliquid's entry into the U.S. market

U.S. customers are still banned from using the Hyperliquid trading platform, which is based in Singapore and does not yet have regulatory approval to operate in the U.S. While President Donald Trump has endorsed Hyperliquid bringing its operations to the U.S., plans are still pending final regulatory approval.

For now, Hyperliquid has found a clever workaround: It has partnered with Payward, the parent company of the Kraken cryptocurrency exchange, to offer perpetual futures trading to a limited number of U.S. customers. Trades occur on the Hyperliquid blockchain platform, but are cleared and settled on Bitnomial, a U.S.-regulated cryptocurrency exchange and clearinghouse owned by Payward.

For most retail investors, though, won't it be easier to use platforms they already know and recognize -- such as Robinhood, Coinbase, and Kalshi -- for their perpetual futures trading?

That's why I'm not as bullish on Hyperliquid's future prospects as others are. It may have the first-mover advantage, but its economic moat simply is not wide or deep enough to entice me. As the gap between Hyperliquid and its rivals narrows, it will likely struggle to outperform Bitcoin over the long haul.
news.summary: Hyperliquid may be soaring, but how much longer can it hold on to its market-leading position?

news.title: Trump warns he has entered ‘deciding mode’ on Iran
news.text:
US President Donald Trump warned on Sunday that he had entered a critical decision phase in the ongoing war with Iran, cautioning that major developments would occur if Tehran failed to change its conduct.

“My question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They had better behave,” Trump told Fox News, detailing his approach to the war. The US president described his current options as wiping the country out, allowing it to “rot” economically, or negotiating a deal, adding that “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future.”

When asked about the UN General Assembly high-level week, which starts on Monday, Trump signalled a willingness to engage diplomatically, saying he would “probably be open” to meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Addressing wider regional hostilities, Trump said Washington remained in constant communication with Yemen’s Houthis following their recent ballistic missile attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, asserting that the group agreed to avoid fighting American forces.

Iran received information that the United States, with the backing of some regional countries, was preparing to resume actions against Tehran, the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC’s) joint military command, said in a statement on Sunday, according to state media.

The military said that any US had been given a “green light” by unnamed regional countries at a joint meeting in Europe to resume action against Tehran.

According to state media, the military added that any US attack would lead to Iranian retaliation “without any limitations or considerations” on US bases and interests. Regional countries involved in any US attack on Iran, the military said, should not expect restraint from Tehran’s armed forces and would be considered complicit and parties to the conflict.

Separately, Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, stated that US President Donald Trump had waged a foolish war on Iran and was foolishly continuing it, IRNA reported.

Rezaei added, however, that Iran “stands ready to give a stronger and more painful response should the US resume military aggression.”

“We have fully prepared ourselves for a decisive war, and the US’ military vulnerabilities are completely known to us. And we are far better prepared this time,” he said, according to IRNA.

The secretary further noted, “Netanyahu plunged Trump into a quagmire.” It was and is in the benefit of the US to accept Iran’s conditions and end the war because the more the conflict drags on, the worse the US’ situation will become, IRNA quoted him as having said.

Iran’s Army Ground Forces Commander Brigadier General Jahanshahi also noted separately that Tehran’s border units remained deployed and on constant alert in various border areas, Press TV reported. Jahanshahi added that the units were prepared to counter any potential threats and to protect the country’s security and territorial integrity.

Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said “one must both fight and negotiate.” He added, “This means at the critical moment we must push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows using our full military might,” Al Jazeera reported.

“However, once we have achieved significant success on the battlefield and the enemy is in a position of weakness, we must use diplomacy to consolidate these gains,” Ghalibaf said.

The speaker noted that Iran’s position in negotiations was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable.”

news.title: 1 shot during encounter with ICE in Austin
news.text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot a man in the torso in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, the latest violent episode to occur as the Trump administration pushes to increase deportations.

State, local and federal law enforcement officers were investigating the episode that took place Sunday under a highway overpass in Northwest Austin. A blue Toyota Corolla punctured by bullets was pulled to the side of the road. Yellow police tape and state trooper vehicles blocked access to the scene.

The area, home to many Latino residents, has seen a recent surge in immigration activity, Austin city officials said at a news conference on Sunday afternoon.

City officials said the person shot was in serious but stable condition at a hospital. Other details remained murky.

It was unclear whether the person had been the target of an immigration operation, but Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the shooting had occurred after a “small foot pursuit.” Officials with the Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not immediately return requests for comment.

“I’m very angry about this,” Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said at the news conference. But, he added, “I’m not surprised at all. It’s happened in other cities with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days and the chaos that we see it performing and fomenting.”

Watson and other city officials called on federal authorities to be open and truthful about the shooting. Information initially reported by DHS in other shootings has, in some cases, proved to be inaccurate.

“There is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said, and there is a reason that people are hurting right now when they hear about this having happened in their city, even before they know all the facts,” said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas.

The violence in Austin was the second Texas ICE shooting in recent months. President Donald Trump has intensified his deportation effort with more targeted operations, which attract less attention, since two civilians were shot and killed during a crackdown in Minneapolis in January.

In July, an ICE agent in Houston shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in the abdomen while he was on his way to work at a construction site with three other men. Araujo, a father, a husband and business owner who had moved to the United States 35 years ago from Mexico, died at a hospital.

Federal officials later said that Araujo had not been the operation’s intended target.

Less than a week after Araujo’s death, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant, was shot and killed by an ICE agent while he headed to work in Biddeford, Maine. Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor ICE has said publicly whether he was the target of an enforcement operation.

More than 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents since Trump took office in January 2025. Six people, including three U.S. citizens, have been killed in those shootings, nearly all of which involved officers firing at people in vehicles.

Months before the fatal shootings of U.S. citizens in Minneapolis, a 23-year-old American man named Ruben Ray Martinez was shot and killed by an ICE officer in South Padre Island, Texas.
